opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the things that jumped out when we extended the time-horizon methodology beyond software engineering and ML research tasks was how different the picture looked for computer-use benchmarks like OSWorld. On the software and reasoning-heavy domains, you see these fairly long time horizons, and a pretty consistent doubling trend. But for general computer use, the kind of thing where the model has to look at a screen, click around in a GUI, navigate an application, the time horizons were much shorter. We're talking tasks that take a human maybe a couple of minutes, and models were still struggling to reliably complete them.

And I think that's striking because intuitively those tasks feel really easy. A person can open a spreadsheet, find the right menu, change some setting, and it's trivial for them. So there's this gap between what feels hard to humans and what's hard for models. Models are quite good at things we consider intellectually demanding, writing code, solving math problems, but the perceptual and motor-ish parts of interacting with a computer, grounding what's on screen, knowing where to click, recovering when something unexpected pops up, those remain bottlenecks.

The other interesting thing was that the rate of improvement looked broadly similar across domains, even though the absolute levels were really different. So you'd have curves offset by a large factor in task length, but roughly parallel. That suggests there's maybe some common underlying driver of progress, and that domains differ more in where they start than in how fast they improve. Of course, I'd want to caveat that heavily. The data for computer use is noisier, the benchmarks weren't designed with human time estimates in mind, so we had to do some work to estimate how long tasks take people. But as a qualitative takeaway, I think it's a useful corrective to the idea that "time horizon" is one single number that captures AI capability. It really depends on the domain.

r001.rationale: The response says computer-use time horizons were much shorter than in software and reasoning-heavy domains, while improvement rates were broadly similar and the curves roughly parallel.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that I think a lot of people found surprising, including me. When we first did the time-horizon analysis, almost all of the data came from software engineering and ML research tasks—things like fixing a bug in a repo, implementing some feature, running an experiment. And on those, the headline result was that the horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months or so, and recently faster than that.

But when you look at general computer-use benchmarks like OSWorld, the striking thing is that the absolute time horizons are much shorter. So on OSWorld, the tasks are things like "change this setting in LibreOffice" or "download this file and put it in this folder"—stuff that would take a human on the order of a minute, maybe a few minutes. And models have been, until fairly recently, pretty bad at those. So you'd have a model that can do a multi-hour software engineering task with reasonable reliability, and then it can't reliably do a two-minute task that involves clicking around in a GUI.

I think there are a few ways to read that. One is just that the models have had way more training signal on coding. There's a ton of code on the internet, there's a ton of RL on coding tasks, and so it's a very optimized domain. Computer use involves looking at screenshots, understanding visual layouts, dealing with latency and UI state, and that's a much newer thing for the labs to be training on. So the gap is plausibly just a measure of how much effort has gone in.

But the other thing that I found interesting is that the trend seems to be similar—the doubling time on computer-use tasks looks roughly comparable, it's just offset. Like, it's lagging by maybe a year or two in terms of where it is on the curve. And that's kind of a nice sanity check that the time-horizon framing isn't just an artifact of software engineering. The same shape shows up in a pretty different domain.

The caveat I'd give is that the human baselines for OSWorld-style tasks are much noisier. A one-minute task has way more relative variance in how long a human takes than a four-hour task does. So the error bars on short-horizon stuff are big, and I wouldn't read too much into the exact numbers. But the qualitative picture—that agents are weirdly jagged, that they can be superhuman at some long tasks and subhuman at some short ones—I think that's real, and it's one of the main reasons I think "time horizon" alone doesn't fully capture capability. You need to know the domain too.

r001.rationale: The response says computer-use tasks have much shorter absolute horizons than software engineering and ML research tasks, while their doubling time looks roughly comparable. That communicates the criterion’s comparison, though it does not name METR or call the other tasks text-only.

You can see models doing these impressive coding tasks, and then on something like OSWorld—using a computer through a graphical interface—they struggle with tasks that would take a human only a few minutes. So I think you have to be careful about treating time horizon as a single, general property of a model. It depends a lot on the domain and on how the model is interacting with the environment.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was how short the tasks still are in human terms. With something like OSWorld, you’re operating a normal computer—clicking around, editing files, using applications—and tasks that a person can finish in a few minutes can still be quite difficult for an agent. That’s a useful counterpoint to seeing models solve very impressive coding or math problems. Being able to do a hard individual step doesn’t necessarily mean you can reliably string together all the steps in an ordinary workflow. Small mistakes compound, and recovering from them is itself part of the task. So I’d be cautious about treating a time horizon measured on coding tasks as a general measure of how long an AI can work autonomously across domains.
